text: Chapter four ends with formatting. A correct report that is hard to scan gets ignored, and formatting is where analysts quietly earn trust.

Start with the report itself. This summary report is grouped by lead source, with subtotals and a record count at the top. In the builder you can reorder columns, drop the ones nobody reads, and in most orgs rename a heading into your team's own language. You can also switch detail rows, subtotals, and the grand total on or off. Collapsed details read like a scorecard.

Now the chart. This properties panel sets the type, title, value, and how groups are sliced. Give the chart a title that states the takeaway, show values so nobody hovers to read them, and combine tiny slices into Others instead of drawing a dozen slivers. Choose the type by question: bars to compare, lines for trends, a donut only for a few parts of a whole.

Before you share anything, run four habits. Trim columns and groupings that don't serve the question. Order rows so the important ones come first. Label headings and titles in plain language. And highlight only the thresholds that drive a decision.

Summary and matrix reports support conditional highlighting on a summary field. You define a few ranges, commonly up to three, and assign each a color. Red below twenty percent, green above fifty, and a manager scans a hundred rows in seconds. Use it sparingly. If everything is colored, nothing stands out.
That closes the charts chapter. Next chapter you carry these charts onto dashboards, starting with what a dashboard component actually is.
